🚨 Scoop: Fearing Mississippi is in play, Senate Republicans are considering spending money there to protect Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith from a surprisingly competitive bid by Democratic district attorney Scott Colom, Axios' Hans Nichols, Marc Caputo and Stef W. Kight report.
 
 
1 big thing: Vance's whine-free zone
 
Vice President Vance speaks at a rally yesterday in Sharonville, Ohio. Photo: Jacquelyn Martin-Pool/Getty Images

Vice President Vance's call for fellow Republicans to "stop whining" about Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial attack ad in Ohio's race for governor showed a key part of his political mindset ahead of his expected run for president in 2028: Never back down.

  • Why it matters: Channeling President Trump, Vance has shown contempt for what he sees as the old-guard GOP's reflex to cave under pressure from Democrats and the media, Axios' Alex Isenstadt writes.

Vance thinks too many Republicans sacrifice allies to make controversies go away, and that giving critics a political scalp only encourages them to demand another, according to people familiar with his thinking.

  • It's an approach with some risk — namely whether Vance, entering a critical period in his political career, has the political muscle to get away with Trump's no-apologies approach.

🔎 Zoom in: Vance defended Ramaswamy yesterday amid bipartisan outrage over an ad featuring the estranged mother of Ramaswamy's Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

  • In the deeply personal ad, Acton's mother calls her daughter a liar, and says Ohioans shouldn't vote for her for governor.
  • Not mentioned in the ad: Acton and her brother were removed from the mother's care as children after Acton accused her stepfather of sexual abuse. Her mother sided with the stepfather, leading to an estrangement that has lasted nearly 50 years.

Vance said he was "disgusted" by fellow Republicans criticizing it, telling them to "stop whining."

  • Asked whether the ad was appropriate, Vance said it was "not really my concern," and that politics is tough.

The other side: Republicans and Democrats have criticized the ad, saying it crossed a moral line.

  • "I would not have run that ad," U.S. Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who appeared alongside Vance and Ramaswamy at the rally, told AP.

2. Trump's war problems surge
 

Traffic passes portraits of Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in Tehran yesterday. Photo: Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images

Twelve days from midterms, President Trump can't escape the unpopular Iran war, which continues to dominate news coverage. Yesterday alone:

  • The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after Election Day, with targets that likely would include Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenal, the N.Y. Times reports.
  • Russian President Vladimir Putin told White House envoy Steve Witkoff he "agrees in principle" to resume trilateral peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. to end the war, Russian and U.S. officials told Axios' Barak Ravid. The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. For now, it seems the only concession Putin agreed to is to negotiate. More from Barak.
  • Putin has never been so close to his goal of normalizing relations with the U.S. "without having to make any compromises on Ukraine," as The Times puts it.
  • The State Department said it ordered non-emergency U.S. government employees to depart Saudi Arabia, "following an uptick in attacks on the kingdom by Iran-backed Houthi militants. The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran," CBS News reports.

🛢️ The big picture: Oil prices are still high (the national average for a gallon of regular is $4.27 today) and stock market futures are shaky due partly to war fears.
 
 
3. 💰 Scoop: AI agents slip into bank accounts
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images

 

Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts — with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios' Madison Mills.

  • Why it matters: AI agents are quickly becoming a nightmare for banks, slipping into their systems faster than they can respond.

Because it's hard to distinguish a human from a bot, banks are blocking the technology and rapidly rewriting their terms of service.

  • Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo are among the banks racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said.

🔭 Zoom in: These are generally situations when an agent or AI assistant accesses a human's account with the user's permission and login credentials.

  • That violates guidelines of most banks, which require humans to log in to their own accounts.

Banking execs fear what agents with login access might do, especially if a user has granted purchase authority or the ability to shift funds.

  • Some banks have tracked activity when agents — programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf — contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions, the people said.

4. 🤖 Exclusive: Main Street's budget AI boom
 
Data: Goldman Sachs. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Small businesses across America are embracing AI, but usage and spending vary dramatically by state, Axios' Herb Scribner writes from an exclusive Goldman Sachs survey of 2,474 small business owners.

  • Why it matters: Companies nationwide, big and small, are figuring out how best to incorporate AI into their workforces and what that means for productivity.

🧮 By the numbers: For all the talk about AI's explosive growth in the enterprise, the survey shows 73% of small businesses are spending $100 or less per month on AI.

  • In Texas, most use AI for marketing copy. In Florida, it's mainly for productivity.

5. 🕶️ Zuck's deal to stay in California
 
Mark Zuckerberg wears Meta glasses last month at the Meta Connect conference in Menlo Park, Calif. Photo: Jeff Chiu/AP

Meta's board struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to keep him living in California after the founder and CEO warned he was considering leaving the state that houses the company's headquarters if voters pass a wealth tax proposal next month, an SEC filing reveals.

  • Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive non-voting shares he can sell to potentially cover a multibillion-dollar tax bill. In return, he committed to remaining a resident of California, or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years, Reuters reports.

Zuckerberg told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because Proposition 40, a ballot measure dubbed the "California wealth tax," could expose him to a massive tax liability.

  • Proposition 40, which asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5% tax on the state's billionaires, is far from certain to pass. The state is home to as many as 250 billionaires, collectively worth more than $2 trillion.

🔎 How it works: Meta will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively creating a two-for-one split to fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining Zuckerberg's control.

  • Zuckerberg can immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill without losing voting control.

6. ⚠️ Least popular in 80 years
 
Graphic: The New York Times

President Trump has the lowest approval rating for any president before a midterm since Harry Truman and the Democrats were routed in 1946, The New York Times' Nate Cohn writes.

  • The final national Times-Siena poll before the election puts Trump's approval rating at 34% — down three points from last month.
Graphic: The New York Times

Likely voters preferred Democratic congressional candidates in their districts by 11 points.

  • Keep reading (gift link).

🗳️ Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 28 House races toward Democrats, pushing the number of seats at least leaning their way to 223 — five more than the 218 needed for a majority.

❎ Turnout for early voting is soaring in many of the states that are expected to decide control of the Senate in next month's midterms, including Texas, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina and Ohio, AP reports.
 
 
7. ⚡ Politico corrects after White House threat
 
President Trump speaks at a campaign rally at Pitt-Greenville Airport on Tuesday in Greenville, N.C. Photo: Evan Vucci/Reuters

The White House counsel's office warned Politico in a Monday letter that it had 48 hours to retract or correct three recent stories about alleged staff drama, or it would suffer unspecified consequences, Axios' Marc Caputo writes.

  • Last night, Politico posted a correction to one of the stories, originally posted last Friday: "An earlier version of this report, including its headline, mischaracterized the role White House chief of staff Susie Wiles played in then-press secretary Katie Zacharia's interview with Sean Hannity on Fox News. POLITICO's follow-up reporting indicates she did not play a direct role in setting up the interview."

Last week's headline: "Susie Wiles helped set up Fox interview ahead of press secretary's exit."

  • The new headline: "Susie Wiles 'offered positive reinforcement' for press secretary's Fox News interview ahead of her exit."
  • Over the weekend, the New York Post reported that internal White House texts show five-day press secretary Katie Zacharia had personally pushed to go on TV ahead of the disastrous Sean Hannity interview. The Post reported that Zacharia texted a White House official: "I'd like to do news hits morning and evening."

📝 The big picture: The White House demand threatens to escalate already tense relations with Politico specifically and, more generally, the press corps that covers President Trump in Washington.

  • Trump last month banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from covering him in the Oval Office and on Air Force One. This week, CNN threatened further legal action to regain access to Air Force One.
  • Trump also blocked all three outlets from the White House grounds, but a judge restored their access on Oct. 13.

🔮 What's next: White House Counsel Will Scharf didn't specify what consequences Politico faces. But a White House official said "all options are on the table" and described Trump's counsel as "uncharacteristically enraged."

  • Trump is highly litigious with media organizations and, advisers say, his appetite for launching lawsuits hasn't diminished.

Politico didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

  • More on the stories.
